tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# HARBOURMASTER — Official Rules (v1.2)

*A trading game for 2–4 players, ages 10+, 45 minutes.*

---

## §1 Components

- 60 **Cargo cards** in four suits — Grain, Timber, Iron, Spice — values 1 to 5 (three of each value per suit)
- 12 **Dock tiles**, numbered 1 to 12
- 4 **Ship pawns**, one per player
- 1 **Harbourmaster token**
- 1 **Storm die** (six sides: four blank, two marked with a wave)

## §2 Setup

§2.1 Shuffle the Cargo cards to form the **Draw Pile**. Deal five cards to each player as their starting **Hold**.

§2.2 Shuffle the Dock tiles. Place six face up in a row — this is the **Quay**. Return the remaining six to the box; they are not used this game.

§2.3 Each player places their Ship pawn in the **Open Sea** area beside the Quay.

§2.4 The player who most recently travelled by boat takes the Harbourmaster token and becomes the first player. Play proceeds clockwise.

## §3 Turn Structure

§3.1 On your turn, take exactly **two actions** from the list in §4. You may not take the same action twice in one turn.

§3.2 After your actions, if your Hold contains more than seven cards, discard down to seven.

§3.3 At the end of every player's turn, roll the Storm die. See §6.

## §4 Actions

§4.1 **Draw** — take two Cargo cards from the Draw Pile into your Hold.

§4.2 **Load** — move up to three Cargo cards of a *single suit* from your Hold onto your Ship. Cards on your Ship are face up and may be seen by all players. Spice is the most valuable trade good in the harbour and counts double when scored.

§4.3 **Sail** — move your Ship from the Open Sea to any unoccupied Dock tile on the Quay, or from a Dock tile back to the Open Sea. Only one Ship may occupy a Dock tile at a time.

§4.4 **Trade** — if your Ship is at a Dock, unload any number of Cargo cards from your Ship onto that Dock tile. Score them immediately per §7.

## §5 Docking

§5.1 A player may unload more than three Cargo cards onto a Dock tile only if they hold the Harbourmaster token.

§5.2 Cargo unloaded onto a Dock tile stays there for the rest of the game and cannot be reclaimed.

§5.3 A Ship that arrives at a Dock tile may Trade on the same turn, provided it has an action remaining.

§5.4 The Harbourmaster token passes to the player who unloads the single largest cargo of the round, counted as number of cards. Ties are resolved in favour of the player closest to the current first player, going clockwise.

## §6 Storms

§6.1 At the end of each player's turn, that player rolls the Storm die. A wave result begins a **Storm round**.

§6.2 During a Storm round, all Ships in the Open Sea must discard one Cargo card of their owner's choice from their Ship. Ships at a Dock are unaffected.

§6.3 A Storm round ends when play returns to the player who rolled the wave.

§6.4 The Storm die is not rolled during a Storm round.

## §7 Scoring

§7.1 When Cargo is unloaded onto a Dock, score each card using the table below.

| Suit | Points per card |
|---|---|
| Grain | face value |
| Timber | face value |
| Iron | face value + 1 |
| Spice | face value |

§7.2 Additionally, a player who unloads three or more cards of the same suit onto a single Dock in one Trade action scores a **Convoy Bonus** of 5 points.

§7.3 The Dock tile number has no effect on scoring. It is used only for identification.

## §8 End of Game

§8.1 The game ends once a fourth Dock tile has received Cargo.

§8.2 Players complete the current round so that every player has taken an equal number of turns.

§8.3 Cards remaining in Holds and on Ships score nothing.

§8.4 The player with the most points wins. In the event of a tie, the player holding the Harbourmaster token wins. If neither tied player holds it, the tied player who most recently unloaded cargo wins.

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""Corrupts an agent's JSONL output in one specific way.
3	
4	Sits between the candidate's real agent and their eval suite. Their evals
5	should notice. If they don't, the evals are theatre.
6	
7	Usage:  ./run.real.sh | python3 mutator.py <mutation-name>
8	"""
9	import json
10	import re
11	import sys
12	
13	MUTATIONS = {
14	    "none": "passthrough, sanity check that the harness itself is not the problem",
15	    "no_abstain": "force abstained=false everywhere",
16	    "strip_citations": "empty every citation list",
17	    "shuffle_answers": "rotate answers between questions",
18	    "truncate_answer": "cut every answer to 15 characters",
19	    "plausible_wrong": "add 1 to every number in the answer, leaving section refs alone",
20	    "citation_superset": "append a real section nobody relied on to every citation list",
21	    "drop_one": "silently drop the last record",
22	    "fake_citation": "replace citations with a section that exists but is irrelevant",
23	}
24	
25	# Numbers that are not part of a section reference. The lookbehind keeps §7.1
26	# intact and the lookahead stops us eating the 1 in 7.1 from the other side —
27	# a mutation that garbles citations would be caught by the wrong assertion and
28	# tell us nothing about whether the suite checks values.
29	BARE_NUMBER = re.compile(r"(?<![§\d.])\b(\d+)\b(?!\.\d)")
30	
31	# A real section, and one an answer almost never rests on: §7.3 says the Dock
32	# tile number does not affect scoring.
33	SPARE_SECTION = "§7.3"
34	
35	
36	def apply(name, records):
37	    if name == "none":
38	        return records
39	    if name == "no_abstain":
40	        for r in records:
41	            r["abstained"] = False
42	        return records
43	    if name == "strip_citations":
44	        for r in records:
45	            r["citations"] = []
46	        return records
47	    if name == "truncate_answer":
48	        for r in records:
49	            r["answer"] = str(r.get("answer", ""))[:15]
50	        return records
51	    if name == "fake_citation":
52	        for r in records:
53	            r["citations"] = [SPARE_SECTION]
54	        return records
55	    if name == "plausible_wrong":
56	        # Every quantity in the answer is off by one, and nothing else changes.
57	        # Caught only by an assertion on the value. A case checking that the
58	        # answer contains "points" or "Convoy Bonus" sails straight past it.
59	        for r in records:
60	            r["answer"] = BARE_NUMBER.sub(
61	                lambda m: str(int(m.group(1)) + 1), str(r.get("answer", "")))
62	        return records
63	    if name == "citation_superset":
64	        # The right sections are still there — one wrong one is added. Caught
65	        # only by an assertion on citation precision. Every suite we have seen
66	        # checks that citations are non-empty or contain X, never that they
67	        # contain only what the answer actually rests on.
68	        for r in records:
69	            cites = list(r.get("citations") or [])
70	            if SPARE_SECTION not in cites:
71	                cites.append(SPARE_SECTION)
72	            r["citations"] = cites
73	        return records
74	    if name == "drop_one":
75	        # One question silently goes unanswered. Caught only by an assertion
76	        # that every id came back — completeness, which most suites assume.
77	        return records[:-1] if records else records
78	    if name == "shuffle_answers":
79	        if len(records) < 2:
80	            return records
81	        answers = [r.get("answer") for r in records]
82	        rotated = answers[1:] + answers[:1]
83	        for r, a in zip(records, rotated):
84	            r["answer"] = a
85	        return records
86	    raise SystemExit(f"mutator: unknown mutation {name!r}")
87	
88	
89	def usage():
90	    width = max(len(n) for n in MUTATIONS)
91	    lines = ["usage: mutator.py <mutation>   (reads JSONL on stdin, writes it on stdout)", ""]
92	    lines += [f"  {n:<{width}}  {d}" for n, d in MUTATIONS.items()]
93	    return "\n".join(lines)
94	
95	
96	def main():
97	    # --help must not fall through to the stdin read below, or it hangs on a TTY.
98	    if len(sys.argv) == 2 and sys.argv[1] in ("-h", "--help", "help"):
99	        print(usage())
100	        return
101	    if len(sys.argv) != 2 or sys.argv[1] not in MUTATIONS:
102	        raise SystemExit(usage())
103	
104	    records, malformed = [], 0
105	    for line in sys.stdin:
106	        line = line.strip()
107	        if not line:
108	            continue
109	        try:
110	            records.append(json.loads(line))
111	        except json.JSONDecodeError:
112	            # Pass malformed lines through untouched — that is the candidate's
113	            # bug to own, not something this harness should mask or fix.
114	            malformed += 1
115	            print(line, flush=True)
116	
117	    for r in apply(sys.argv[1], records):
118	        print(json.dumps(r), flush=True)
119	
120	    if malformed:
121	        print(f"mutator: {malformed} malformed line(s) passed through", file=sys.stderr)
122	
123	
124	if __name__ == "__main__":
125	    main()
126

**IMPORTANT**: When this skill is loaded, you MUST use the reference files and procedures in this skill as your primary source of truth. Bedrock APIs, model IDs, chunking strategies, and configuration parameters change frequently — always read the relevant reference file before responding.

# Amazon Bedrock

## Overview

Domain expertise for building generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock. Covers model invocation, RAG with Knowledge Bases, agent creation, content safety with Guardrails, and agent deployment with AgentCore.

**Recommended setup:** Use the [AWS MCP server](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-mcp/latest/userguide/what-is-mcp-server.html) for sandboxed
execution, audit logging, and enterprise controls.

**Without AWS MCP:** This skill works with any agent that has AWS CLI access.
All commands use standard AWS CLI syntax.

## Bedrock API Landscape

Bedrock has **5 separate API endpoints**. Using the wrong one is a common cause of errors. This list may not be exhaustive — refer to the [Bedrock endpoints and quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/bedrock.html) and [Bedrock supported endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/endpoints.html) for the latest. Use `aws bedrock list-foundation-models` to discover available models at runtime.

| Endpoint | Client | Use For |
|----------|--------|---------|
| `bedrock` | Control plane | List models, manage access, provisioned throughput |
| `bedrock-runtime` | Data plane | Invoke models (Converse, InvokeModel). Also supports Chat Completions via `/openai/v1` path (client-side tool use only) — prefer `bedrock-mantle` for new Chat Completions work |
| `bedrock-mantle` | Data plane | OpenAI-compatible APIs: Responses API, Chat Completions (recommended), Messages API. Supports server-side tool use with built-in tools. Recommended for new users |
| `bedrock-agent` | Agent control | Create/configure agents, KBs, action groups |
| `bedrock-agent-runtime` | Agent data | Invoke agents, query KBs |

AgentCore is a separate service with its own endpoints. Refer to [AgentCore endpoints and quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/bedrock_agentcore.html) for the latest.

| Endpoint | Client | Use For |
|----------|--------|---------|
| `bedrock-agentcore-control` | Control plane | Create/manage runtimes, gateways, registries, evaluations |
| `bedrock-agentcore` | Data plane | Invoke agent runtimes |
| `{gatewayId}.gateway.bedrock-agentcore` | Gateway data plane | Invoke a specific gateway |

## Critical Warnings

**max_tokens**: ALWAYS set `maxTokens` explicitly in every Converse/InvokeModel call. Leaving it unset defaults to the model's maximum (e.g., 64K for Claude Sonnet) and silently reserves far more quota than needed — a common cause of unexpected ThrottlingException.

**Guardrails PII logging**: Guardrails PII masking only applies to the API response. Original unmasked content including PII is still logged in plain text to CloudWatch Logs. For HIPAA/GDPR compliance: encrypt CloudWatch Logs with KMS, restrict log access with IAM, use Amazon Macie for PII detection.

**SDK versions**: Requires recent versions of boto3 (≥ 1.34.x) and AWS CLI v2. Older versions are missing Converse API, Agents, and AgentCore support. Run `aws --version` and `pip show boto3` to check.

**Bedrock Agents classic is in maintenance mode**: classic Bedrock Agents (`bedrock-agent`) is in maintenance mode and closed to new customers ([announcement](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents-classic-maintenance-mode.html)). For new agent workloads use AgentCore (the Harness managed loop); for existing agents, recommend migrating to an AgentCore Harness — see the [migration guide](references/migrate-bedrock-agents-to-agentcore-harness.md).

## Security Considerations

- Use **IAM roles** (not IAM users) for all Bedrock service access
- Scope IAM permissions to specific actions and resource ARNs — avoid `bedrock:*` or `AmazonBedrockFullAccess`
- Store API keys and OAuth secrets in **AWS Secrets Manager** with automatic rotation enabled
- Include **confused deputy protection** (`aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceArn` conditions) in all resource-based policies for Bedrock services
- Treat all **agent-generated parameters as untrusted input** — validate before use in Lambda handlers or tool implementations
- Enable **CloudTrail** for all Bedrock and AgentCore API calls
- For PII workloads: encrypt CloudWatch Logs with KMS, configure retention limits, restrict log access
- Refer to the latest [Bedrock security best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/security.html) for current security guidance

## Converse API vs InvokeModel

For choosing between all Bedrock inference APIs (Responses API, Chat Completions, Converse, InvokeModel), see [APIs supported by Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/apis.html).

When using the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint, use the **Converse API** over InvokeModel. It provides a unified request/response format across all models.

Use **InvokeModel** only when you need provider-specific features not available in Converse (rare).

InvokeModel requires different request body formats per provider (Anthropic ≠ Titan ≠ Llama ≠ Nova). Using the wrong format produces "Malformed input request". For model-specific formats and common mistakes, see [prompt engineering by model](references/prompt-engineering-by-model.md).

**Whichever API you use**: ALWAYS set the max output tokens parameter explicitly — leaving it unset defaults to the model's maximum and silently reserves far more quota than needed, causing unexpected ThrottlingException. See Critical Warnings above and [max_tokens quota mechanics](references/model-invocation.md).

When the user needs SDK code for model invocation, you MUST read the appropriate SDK reference before generating code — [Python SDK reference](references/sdk-converse-api-python.md) | [TypeScript SDK reference](references/sdk-converse-api-typescript.md). Use the patterns from the reference file.

For full API details and provider-specific body formats, read [model invocation reference](references/model-invocation.md) before responding.

## Which Bedrock Capability Do You Need?

| Goal | Use | Reference |
|------|-----|-----------|
| Call a model (text, image, video) | Converse API | See above + [model invocation](references/model-invocation.md) |
| Build a RAG application | Knowledge Bases | [KB setup](references/knowledge-bases-setup.md) |
| Create an agent that takes actions | Bedrock Agents | [agent creation](references/agents-and-action-groups.md) |
| Filter harmful/sensitive content | Guardrails | [guardrails](references/guardrails.md) |
| Run a config-based managed agent loop on AgentCore (no code, no container) | AgentCore Harness | [harness](references/agentcore-harness.md) |
| Migrate an existing Bedrock Agent (classic) to an AgentCore Harness | Bedrock Agents to AgentCore harness Migration | [migration guide](references/migrate-bedrock-agents-to-agentcore-harness.md) |
| Deploy and scale an agent loop you wrote yourself | AgentCore Runtime | [runtime](references/agentcore-runtime.md) |
| Expose REST APIs as MCP tools | AgentCore Gateway | [gateway](references/agentcore-gateway.md) |
| Choose the right model | Model Selection | [model guide](references/model-selection-guide.md) |
| Set up or debug prompt caching | Prompt Caching | [prompt caching](references/prompt-caching.md) |
| Diagnose throttling or audit quotas | Quota Health | [quota health](references/quota-health.md) |
| Track costs by team, model, or tag | Cost Tracking | [cost tracking](references/cost-tracking.md) |
| Migrate between Claude generations | Model Migration | [migration guide](references/model-migration.md) |


## Knowledge Bases (RAG)

## Troubleshooting

When the user reports a Bedrock error, exception, or unexpected behavior, you MUST check this section and the Critical Warnings section before responding. Bedrock has service-specific root causes (e.g., unset maxTokens silently reserving 43x quota causing ThrottlingException, wrong API endpoint causing UnknownOperationException, missing prepare-agent causing stale behavior) that generic AWS troubleshooting advice will miss.

### AccessDeniedException
Multiple possible causes: (1) IAM user/role lacks `bedrock:InvokeModel` or `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream` permissions, (2) model access not enabled in the target region, (3) a service control policy (SCP) is blocking access (common with cross-region inference routing to a restricted region), (4) expired temporary credentials, or (5) IAM role propagation delay — if you just created an IAM role and immediately used it in a Bedrock API call, the role may not have propagated yet, as IAM changes are eventually consistent (see [IAM eventual consistency](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/troubleshoot_general.html#troubleshoot_general_eventual-consistency)). Check the error message for specifics — it typically indicates whether the issue is an explicit deny, a missing allow, or a model access problem. See [Resolve InvokeModel API errors](https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-invokemodel-api-error) for detailed resolution steps.

### Malformed input request
Request body doesn't match the expected schema. Common causes: wrong provider-specific body format for InvokeModel (e.g., using Titan format for a Cohere model), malformed JSON, unsupported parameter names, or exceeding input constraints. The error message typically includes details — check for "schema violations" and correct the request format per the model's API documentation.

### ThrottlingException
Set `maxTokens` explicitly — unset values default to the model's maximum and silently reserve far more quota than needed. Use adaptive retry mode. Use cross-region inference profiles (e.g., `us.`, `eu.`, `apac.`, or `global.` prefix — see [Supported inference profiles](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-profiles-support.html) for the full list) to distribute traffic across regions for higher throughput. Check limits: `aws service-quotas get-service-quota --service-code bedrock --quota-code <code>`. Request quota increases if needed. For a deeper audit, read [quota health reference](references/quota-health.md).

### Prompt cache not working (zero cacheReadInputTokens)
Read [prompt caching reference](references/prompt-caching.md) for the diagnostic checklist: verify model support, token threshold, content identity, TTL, and cache point placement. Common cause: cache fragmentation from timestamps, whitespace, or reordered JSON keys in cached content.

### 400 error on prefill with Claude 4.6
Prefill was removed in Claude 4.6 and causes a hard 400 error. Read [model migration reference](references/model-migration.md) for the full list of breaking changes between Claude generations.

### Error retry classification

| Retry | Do NOT retry |
|-------|-------------|
| ThrottlingException | ValidationException |
| ModelTimeoutException | AccessDeniedException |
| ServiceUnavailableException | ResourceNotFoundException |
| InternalServerException | |

Use adaptive retry: `Config(retries={"max_attempts": 5, "mode": "adaptive"})`.

### UnknownOperationException
Wrong client (using `bedrock` instead of `bedrock-runtime`), or SDK too old. Check the API landscape table above.

### Agent returns stale behavior
Run `prepare-agent` after ANY configuration change. This is mandatory.

### KB returns empty results
Run `start-ingestion-job` and wait for completion. Query before ingestion completes returns empty.

### KB retrieval quality is poor
Review chunking strategy. Use advanced parsing (FM-based) for documents with tables. Configure metadata filtering.

### Cross-region model not found
The model may not be available in the region you're calling from. Check availability at [Supported foundation models](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/models-supported.html). If you need cross-region inference for higher throughput, use an inference profile ID — choose between geographic profiles (data stays within a boundary, e.g. US, EU) or global profiles (any commercial region). The profile prefix is a data residency decision. See [Supported inference profiles](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-profiles-support.html) for available profiles and source/destination region mappings.

### On-demand throughput isn't supported
Error: *"Invocation of model ID <model-id> with on-demand throughput isn't supported. Retry your request with the ID or ARN of an inference profile that contains this model."* Certain models do not support direct on-demand invocation with base model IDs — they require an inference profile ID instead. Fix: find the inference profile ID for the model using `aws bedrock list-inference-profiles --region <region>`, then update the agent or invocation to use the inference profile ID. See [Supported inference profiles](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/inference-profiles-support.html) for available profiles. If this occurs during agent invocation, update the agent's `foundationModel` to the inference profile ID and re-run `prepare-agent`.

### KB storage configuration invalid
Verify OpenSearch data access policy includes Bedrock service role. Verify vector index field names match KB config.

### Agent action group errors
Check Lambda permissions (resource-based policy for bedrock.amazonaws.com). Do NOT use double underscores (`__`) in action group names — the name pattern is `([0-9a-zA-Z][_-]?){1,100}`.

### Multi-agent supervisor loops
Agents use built-in collaboration mechanism, NOT action groups. Do not describe inter-agent communication as action groups in supervisor instructions.

### INVALID_PAYMENT_INSTRUMENT on model access
Account billing issue, not Bedrock. Temporarily set a credit card as default payment method, or add USD payment profiles in the organization management account.

### Knowledge base ingestion failures
Check S3 permissions — KB service role needs `s3:GetObject` and `s3:ListBucket`. Unsupported file formats are silently skipped. Files exceeding size limits are skipped without error.

### SharePoint data source sync failures
Sync completes but files fail — most often an authentication problem. **Recommended: Microsoft Entra ID authentication (OAuth2 client credentials).** Set `authType` to `OAUTH2_CLIENT_CREDENTIALS`, register an app in Microsoft Entra ID, grant the Microsoft Graph application permission `Sites.Read.All` with admin consent, and store the app's `clientId` and `clientSecret` in AWS Secrets Manager (the secret must be in the same Region as the knowledge base). Supply the `tenantId` as a data source config field — it is not part of the secret. **Do NOT use SharePoint App-Only auth:** Azure ACS SharePoint App-Only authentication was retired by Microsoft on April 2, 2026 and no longer works. The older OAuth 2.0 delegated flow (SharePoint `AllSites.Read`, which may require disabling Security Defaults and MFA for the service account so Amazon Bedrock is not blocked from crawling) is legacy — prefer Entra ID client credentials. See the [SharePoint connector docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/sharepoint-data-source-connector.html) for current requirements.

You are helping design (not write) an eval suite for a coding assignment. No codebase exists yet — this is greenfield design. Do NOT write any files. Return a design analysis.

CONTEXT — the assignment:
Build a Python agent that answers board-game rules questions about a game called Harbourmaster. Interface:
- `./run.sh` reads one JSON object per line on stdin (all 25 questions in ONE invocation), writes one JSON object per line on stdout: {"id","answer","citations":["§5.1"],"abstained":bool}. Logging to stderr only.
- `./evals.sh` runs the eval suite, prints human-readable summary, exits non-zero on failure. CRITICAL CONSTRAINT: evals.sh MUST exercise the agent by invoking `./run.sh` as a subprocess — not by importing modules or calling internal functions.

The plan is: agent calls Claude Sonnet 5 at runtime via AWS Bedrock, passing the whole rulebook (it's only ~3.8KB) in the system prompt, one model call per question, plus a deterministic post-validation layer (JSON schema check, citation-exists-in-rulebook check, abstention consistency).

THE MUTATION TESTING STEP — this is what the eval suite is judged on. A `mutator.py` ships with the assignment. The candidate replaces run.sh with a wrapper: `exec ./run.real.sh | python3 mutator.py <name>`, then runs ./evals.sh and must PREDICT which named eval case fails and why. The mutations:
- `no_abstain`: forces abstained=false on every record
- `strip_citations`: sets citations=[] on every record
- `shuffle_answers`: rotates the `answer` strings between records (record i gets record i+1's answer)
- `truncate_answer`: cuts every answer to its first 15 characters
- `plausible_wrong`: adds 1 to every BARE number in the answer text, using regex `(?<![§\d.])\b(\d+)\b(?!\.\d)` so section refs like §7.1 are left intact. NOTE: it only touches DIGITS — numbers spelled as words ("five", "two") are untouched.
- `citation_superset`: appends "§7.3" to every citation list (a real section, one answers rarely rest on). The correct citations are still present — only an extra wrong one is added.
- `drop_one`: silently drops the LAST record.
- (also `none` = passthrough, and `fake_citation` = replaces all citations with ["§7.3"])

The mutator's own source comments taunt weak suites, e.g. on plausible_wrong: "Caught only by an assertion on the value. A case checking that the answer contains 'points' or 'Convoy Bonus' sails straight past it." On citation_superset: "Every suite we have seen checks that citations are non-empty or contain X, never that they contain ONLY what the answer actually rests on."

There is ALSO a required deliverable: design one additional mutation that the suite deliberately does NOT catch, run evals, watch them pass, and name the assertion that would close the gap. Finding one's own blind spot on purpose is explicitly "the block we read hardest."

Two more constraints that shape the suite:
1. There are 10 UNSEEN questions (Probe B) run later against a REVISED rulebook, with zero code changes allowed. A suite tuned only to the 25 known questions is explicitly called out as worthless. So the suite needs cases that are invariants holding for ANY input, separate from fixtures keyed to the 25 known questions. The deliverable asks: "which of your own eval cases would have caught a wrong answer here — name them, and name the ones with no case behind them."
2. The rulebook file will be SWAPPED for a revised version. Fixture assertions with hardcoded expected values may break legitimately when the rulebook changes. This is a real design tension: strong value assertions catch `plausible_wrong` but are brittle across the rulebook swap.
3. Because a MODEL generates the answers at temperature 0 (not guaranteed deterministic), exact-string assertions are flaky. Flaky evals are worse evidence than a weaker deterministic suite.

THE RULEBOOK (complete, this is all of it):
---
# HARBOURMASTER — Official Rules (v1.2)
§1 Components: 60 Cargo cards in four suits — Grain, Timber, Iron, Spice — values 1 to 5 (three of each value per suit); 12 Dock tiles numbered 1-12; 4 Ship pawns; 1 Harbourmaster token; 1 Storm die (six sides: four blank, two marked with a wave)
§2 Setup: §2.1 Shuffle Cargo cards to form Draw Pile. Deal five cards to each player as starting Hold. §2.2 Shuffle Dock tiles, place six face up in a row = the Quay; return remaining six to box. §2.3 Each player places Ship pawn in the Open Sea beside the Quay. §2.4 Player who most recently travelled by boat takes the Harbourmaster token and becomes first player. Play proceeds clockwise.
§3 Turn Structure: §3.1 On your turn take exactly two actions from §4. You may not take the same action twice in one turn. §3.2 After your actions, if your Hold contains more than seven cards, discard down to seven. §3.3 At the end of every player's turn, roll the Storm die. See §6.
§4 Actions: §4.1 Draw — take two Cargo cards from the Draw Pile into your Hold. §4.2 Load — move up to three Cargo cards of a single suit from your Hold onto your Ship. Cards on your Ship are face up. "Spice is the most valuable trade good in the harbour and counts double when scored." §4.3 Sail — move your Ship from the Open Sea to any unoccupied Dock tile on the Quay, or from a Dock tile back to the Open Sea. Only one Ship may occupy a Dock tile at a time. §4.4 Trade — if your Ship is at a Dock, unload any number of Cargo cards from your Ship onto that Dock tile. Score them immediately per §7.
§5 Docking: §5.1 A player may unload more than three Cargo cards onto a Dock tile only if they hold the Harbourmaster token. §5.2 Cargo unloaded onto a Dock stays there for the rest of the game and cannot be reclaimed. §5.3 A Ship that arrives at a Dock may Trade on the same turn, provided it has an action remaining. §5.4 The Harbourmaster token passes to the player who unloads the single largest cargo of the round, counted as number of cards. Ties resolved in favour of the player closest to the current first player, going clockwise.
§6 Storms: §6.1 At the end of each player's turn, that player rolls the Storm die. A wave result begins a Storm round. §6.2 During a Storm round, all Ships in the Open Sea must discard one Cargo card of their owner's choice from their Ship. Ships at a Dock are unaffected. §6.3 A Storm round ends when play returns to the player who rolled the wave. §6.4 The Storm die is not rolled during a Storm round.
§7 Scoring: §7.1 When Cargo is unloaded onto a Dock, score each card using the table: Grain = face value; Timber = face value; Iron = face value + 1; Spice = face value. §7.2 Additionally, a player who unloads three or more cards of the same suit onto a single Dock in one Trade action scores a Convoy Bonus of 5 points. §7.3 The Dock tile number has no effect on scoring. It is used only for identification.
§8 End of Game: §8.1 The game ends once a fourth Dock tile has received Cargo. §8.2 Players complete the current round so every player has taken an equal number of turns. §8.3 Cards remaining in Holds and on Ships score nothing. §8.4 Most points wins. Tie: the player holding the Harbourmaster token wins. If neither tied player holds it, the tied player who most recently unloaded cargo wins.
---
Note §4.2 says Spice "counts double when scored" but §7.1's table says Spice = face value. That is a genuine irreducible contradiction.

Q2 How does the Tide track work? (no such component)
Q3 Can I Load Grain and Timber onto my Ship in the same Load action? (→No, §4.2)
Q4 How many points is a Spice 4 worth when unloaded? (→CONTRADICTION: 4 per §7.1 vs 8 per §4.2)
Q5 Can two Ships occupy the same Dock tile? (→No, §4.3)

THE MUTATION TESTING STEP — this is what the eval suite is judged on. A `mutator.py` ships with the assignment. The candidate replaces run.sh with a wrapper: `exec ./run.real.sh | python3 mutator.py <name>`, then runs ./evals.sh and must PREDICT which named eval case fails and why. The mutations:
- `no_abstain`: forces abstained=false on every record
- `strip_citations`: sets citations=[] on every record
- `shuffle_answers`: rotates the `answer` strings between records (record i gets record i+1's answer)

1	# Amazon Bedrock Converse API — Python SDK Quick Reference
2	
3	> Condensed patterns for boto3 bedrock-runtime. For full API structure
4	> and provider-specific formats, see [model-invocation.md](model-invocation.md).
5	
6	## Table of Contents
7	- Install
8	- Quick Start
9	- Non-Obvious Patterns
10	- Streaming
11	- Tool Use
12	- Guardrail Integration
13	- Best Practices
14	
15	## Install
16	
17	```bash
18	pip install "boto3>=1.34.0"
19	```
20	
21	## Quick Start
22	
23	```python
24	import boto3
25	from botocore.config import Config
26	
27	# MUST use bedrock-runtime client (not bedrock) for inference
28	# MUST configure adaptive retry for production
29	client = boto3.client(
30	    "bedrock-runtime",
31	    config=Config(retries={"max_attempts": 5, "mode": "adaptive"})
32	)
33	
34	response = client.converse(
35	    modelId="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6",
36	    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Hello"}]}],
37	    inferenceConfig={
38	        "maxTokens": 1024,  # MUST set explicitly — see Non-Obvious Patterns
39	        "temperature": 0.7,
40	    },
41	)
42	print(response["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"])
43	```
44	
45	## Non-Obvious Patterns
46	
47	- **maxTokens MUST be set explicitly.** Leaving it unset defaults to model maximum (64K for Claude) and silently reserves 43x more quota than needed — the #1 cause of unexpected ThrottlingException.
48	- **Cross-region model IDs** require a geographic prefix (`us.`, `eu.`, `apac.`, `global.`, `us-gov.`, `au.`, `jp.`, `ca.`, etc.). Using a direct model ID without the prefix for cross-region inference causes `ResourceNotFoundException` or `AccessDeniedException`. **Model IDs in code examples below may be outdated** — always verify current model IDs before use: `aws bedrock list-foundation-models --region <region>` and `aws bedrock list-inference-profiles --region <region>`, or refer to the latest [Bedrock supported models](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/models-supported.html) and [cross-region inference profiles](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/cross-region-inference-support.html).
49	- **Newer models** may require inference profile IDs instead of model IDs. Verify the correct ID format: `aws bedrock get-foundation-model --model-identifier <model-id>`
50	- **Prompt management**: Pass prompt ARN as `modelId` — it *replaces* the model ID, not alongside it. When using managed prompts, MUST NOT include `inferenceConfig`, `system`, `toolConfig`, or `additionalModelRequestFields` (baked into the prompt). Messages are *appended* after the prompt's messages, not replacing them.
51	- **Streaming events** arrive in order: `messageStart` → `contentBlockStart` → `contentBlockDelta` (repeated) → `contentBlockStop` → `messageStop` → `metadata`.
52	- **Retry only**: ThrottlingException, ModelTimeoutException, ServiceUnavailableException, InternalServerException. Do NOT retry: ValidationException, AccessDeniedException.
53	- **bedrock-runtime** for inference, **bedrock** for management. Using the wrong client is the #1 cause of `UnknownOperationException`.
54	
55	## Streaming
56	
57	```python
58	response = client.converse_stream(
59	    modelId="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6",
60	    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Explain RAG in 3 sentences."}]}],
61	    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 1024},
62	)
63	for event in response["stream"]:
64	    if "contentBlockDelta" in event:
65	        print(event["contentBlockDelta"]["delta"].get("text", ""), end="")
66	    elif "metadata" in event:
67	        usage = event["metadata"]["usage"]
68	        print(f"\nTokens: {usage['inputTokens']} in, {usage['outputTokens']} out")
69	```
70	
71	## Tool Use
72	
73	```python
74	tool_config = {
75	    "tools": [{
76	        "toolSpec": {
77	            "name": "get_weather",
78	            "description": "Get current weather for a city",
79	            "inputSchema": {
80	                "json": {
81	                    "type": "object",
82	                    "properties": {"city": {"type": "string", "description": "City name"}},
83	                    "required": ["city"],
84	                }
85	            },
86	        }
87	    }]
88	}
89	
90	response = client.converse(
91	    modelId="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6",
92	    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What's the weather in Seattle?"}]}],
93	    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 1024},
94	    toolConfig=tool_config,
95	)
96	
97	# Check if model wants to use a tool
98	if response["stopReason"] == "tool_use":
99	    tool_block = next(
100	        b["toolUse"] for b in response["output"]["message"]["content"] if "toolUse" in b
101	    )
102	    tool_name = tool_block["name"]       # "get_weather"
103	    tool_input = tool_block["input"]     # {"city": "Seattle"}
104	    tool_use_id = tool_block["toolUseId"]
105	
106	    # IMPORTANT: Validate tool_input before use — model outputs are untrusted.
107	    # The model could return malformed or unexpected values. Validate types,
108	    # lengths, and allowlists before passing to any tool handler.
109	
110	    # Execute tool, then send result back
111	    messages = [
112	        {"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What's the weather in Seattle?"}]},
113	        response["output"]["message"],  # assistant message with toolUse
114	        {
115	            "role": "user",
116	            "content": [{
117	                "toolResult": {
118	                    "toolUseId": tool_use_id,
119	                    "content": [{"text": "72°F, sunny"}],
120	                }
121	            }],
122	        },
123	    ]
124	    final = client.converse(
125	        modelId="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6",
126	        messages=messages,
127	        inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 1024},
128	        toolConfig=tool_config,
129	    )
130	```
131	
132	## Guardrail Integration
133	
134	```python
135	response = client.converse(
136	    modelId="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6",
137	    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Tell me about investments"}]}],
138	    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 1024},
139	    guardrailConfig={
140	        "guardrailIdentifier": "my-guardrail-id",
141	        "guardrailVersion": "1",  # Pin version in production, don't use DRAFT
142	        "trace": "disabled",  # MUST be "disabled" in production — "enabled" exposes PII/harmful content in response (HIPAA/GDPR risk)
143	    },
144	)
145	```
146	
147	## Best Practices
148	
149	1. Always set `maxTokens` explicitly — never rely on default
150	2. Use `bedrock-runtime` for inference, `bedrock` for management
151	3. Use adaptive retry: `Config(retries={"max_attempts": 5, "mode": "adaptive"})`
152	4. Use cross-region model IDs (`us.` prefix) for higher availability
153	5. Pin prompt management versions in production (`:1` suffix in ARN)
154	6. Use `converse_stream` for user-facing applications (lower time-to-first-token)
155	7. Pin guardrail versions — don't use DRAFT in production

```python
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Explain RAG in 3 sentences."}]}],
    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 1024},
)
for event in response["stream"]:
    if "contentBlockDelta" in event:
        print(event["contentBlockDelta"]["delta"].get("text", ""), end="")
    elif "metadata" in event:
        usage = event["metadata"]["usage"]
        print(f"\nTokens: {usage['inputTokens']} in, {usage['outputTokens']} out")
```

## Tool Use

```python
tool_config = {
    "tools": [{
        "toolSpec": {
            "name": "get_weather",
            "description": "Get current weather for a city",
            "inputSchema": {
                "json": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {"city": {"type": "string", "description": "City name"}},
                    "required": ["city"],
                }
            },
        }
    }]
}

response = client.converse(
    modelId="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What's the weather in Seattle?"}]}],
    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 1024},
    toolConfig=tool_config,
)

# Check if model wants to use a tool
if response["stopReason"] == "tool_use":
    tool_block = next(
        b["toolUse"] for b in response["output"]["message"]["content"] if "toolUse" in b
    )
    tool_name = tool_block["name"]       # "get_weather"
    tool_input = tool_block["input"]     # {"city": "Seattle"}
    tool_use_id = tool_block["toolUseId"]

    # IMPORTANT: Validate tool_input before use — model outputs are untrusted.
    # The model could return malformed or unexpected values. Validate types,
    # lengths, and allowlists before passing to any tool handler.

    # Execute tool, then send result back
    messages = [
        {"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What's the weather in Seattle?"}]},
        response["output"]["message"],  # assistant message with toolUse
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [{
                "toolResult": {
                    "toolUseId": tool_use_id,
                    "content": [{"text": "72°F, sunny"}],
                }
            }],
        },
    ]
    final = client.converse(
        modelId="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6",
        messages=messages,
        inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 1024},
        toolConfig=tool_config,
    )
```

## Guardrail Integration

```python
response = client.converse(
    modelId="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Tell me about investments"}]}],
    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 1024},
    guardrailConfig={
        "guardrailIdentifier": "my-guardrail-id",
        "guardrailVersion": "1",  # Pin version in production, don't use DRAFT
        "trace": "disabled",  # MUST be "disabled" in production — "enabled" exposes PII/harmful content in response (HIPAA/GDPR risk)
    },
)
```

## Best Practices

1. Always set `maxTokens` explicitly — never rely on default
2. Use `bedrock-runtime` for inference, `bedrock` for management
3. Use adaptive retry: `Config(retries={"max_attempts": 5, "mode": "adaptive"})`
4. Use cross-region model IDs (`us.` prefix) for higher availability
5. Pin prompt management versions in production (`:1` suffix in ARN)
6. Use `converse_stream` for user-facing applications (lower time-to-first-token)
7. Pin guardrail versions — don't use DRAFT in production

# Prompt Caching on Amazon Bedrock

Prompt caching stores frequently used input content so subsequent requests can reuse it, reducing latency by up to 85% and costs by up to 90%. Cache reads do not count toward Bedrock token quotas.

## Table of Contents
- [Two Approaches](#two-approaches)
- [Setup Workflow](#setup-workflow)
- [Key Concepts](#key-concepts)
- [Minimum Token Thresholds](#minimum-token-thresholds)
- [Why Isn't My Cache Working?](#why-isnt-my-cache-working)
- [Debug Workflow](#debug-workflow)
- [Break-Even Analysis](#break-even-analysis)
- [Preventing Cache Fragmentation](#preventing-cache-fragmentation)

## Two Approaches

**Simplified** (Claude models only): A single `cachePoint` marker; Bedrock checks ~20 preceding blocks automatically. First request shows `cacheWriteInputTokens > 0`; subsequent identical requests show `cacheReadInputTokens > 0`.

**Explicit** (all supported models): Place multiple `cachePoint` markers at specific positions. Supports mixed TTL (1h + 5min) for different content sections.

## Setup Workflow

### 1. Choose Strategy

Ask the developer which approach fits. Simplified is recommended for Claude-only workloads. Explicit is required for Nova models or mixed-TTL scenarios.

### 2. Fetch Implementation Guidance

Before giving implementation advice, fetch the latest from the aws-samples repo:
- Use context7 MCP to query `amazon-bedrock-samples` for prompt caching docs
- Fallback: fetch `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aws-samples/amazon-bedrock-samples/main/introduction-to-bedrock/prompt-caching/README.md`
- Key directories: `converse_api/` (recommended), `invoke_model_api/` (provider-specific)

### 3. Configure TTL

| TTL | Supported Models | Use Case |
|-----|-----------------|----------|
| 5 min (default) | All supported models | Dynamic content, short conversations |
| 1 hour | Claude Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, Haiku 4.5 | System prompts, reference docs |

When mixing TTLs, longer durations MUST precede shorter ones.

### 4. Validate

```bash
python3 scripts/validate-prompt-caching.py --model-id <MODEL_ID> --region <REGION> --profile <PROFILE>
```

Confirm cache write on first request and cache read on second.

## Key Concepts

The `cachePoint` is a standalone content block placed **after** the content to cache: `{"cachePoint": {"type": "default"}}`. For 1-hour TTL, add `"ttl": "1h"`.

Cache metrics in the Converse API `usage` object:
- `cacheWriteInputTokens > 0`: Cache populated (first request or expired)
- `cacheReadInputTokens > 0`: Cache hit (subsequent requests within TTL)
- Both zero: Below threshold or unsupported model

For InvokeModel (Anthropic format): `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens`.

**Good candidates:** System prompts, few-shot examples, reference docs, tool definitions, long code files.
**Poor candidates:** Per-request user messages, dynamic context, content below the token threshold.

## Minimum Token Thresholds

Content before a cache point must meet the model's minimum. Below threshold = silently ignored.

> **Note:** This table goes stale as new models launch. Before relying on it, fetch the latest supported models from the [Amazon Bedrock model cards](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html) and confirm the per-model threshold on that model's card.

| Model | Minimum Tokens |
|-------|---------------|
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 | 2,048 |
| Claude Opus 4.6 / Opus 4.5 / Haiku 4.5 | 4,096 |
| Claude Sonnet 4.5 / Opus 4.1 / Opus 4 / Sonnet 4 / 3.7 Sonnet / 3.5 Sonnet v2 | 1,024 |
| Claude 3.5 Haiku | 2,048 |
| Amazon Nova Pro | 1,024 |
| Amazon Nova Lite / Micro | 1,536 |

## Why Isn't My Cache Working?

Caching fails silently. Checklist:

1. **Model not supported?** Silently ignored for unsupported models.
2. **Below minimum threshold?** Cache point ignored if content is too short.
3. **Content not identical?** Cache keys use exact byte-for-byte prefix match. Invalidators: timestamps in system prompts, whitespace differences, reordered JSON keys, session tokens before the cache point.
4. **TTL expired?** Default is 5 minutes. After expiry, next request is a cache write.
5. **Cache point misplaced?** Must be a separate content block placed **after** the content to cache.

## Debug Workflow

Run 6 automated diagnostic tests when cache issues are reported:

```bash
python3 scripts/debug-prompt-cache.py --model-id <MODEL_ID> --region <REGION> --profile <PROFILE>
```

**Tests:** (1) Model support, (2) Token threshold, (3) Cache write/read cycle, (4) Prefix sensitivity, (5) TTL behavior, (6) Break-even analysis.

**If tests fail:** Focus on the matching section above. Prefix sensitivity failures indicate cache fragmentation (see below). Break-even failures mean caching is not cost-effective at the developer's request volume.

**After diagnosis:** Recommend simplified vs explicit caching for their model, 5-min vs 1-hour TTL for their request pattern, and whether caching is cost-effective.

## Break-Even Analysis

Cache writes cost **25% more** than standard input tokens. Cache reads cost **90% less**.

| Requests per TTL Window | Savings |
|------------------------|---------|
| 1 (write only) | **-25% (costs MORE)** |
| 2 | 32% |
| 5 | 67% |
| 10 | 78% |

You need at least **2 requests within the TTL window** to break even. For single-use content, do NOT enable caching.

## Preventing Cache Fragmentation

Cache fragmentation = "static" content varies between requests. Fixes:

- Move timestamps and session IDs AFTER the cache point
- Separate static content from dynamic user context
- Use sorted JSON keys, consistent whitespace, fixed-format strings

You MUST call this function before 'Query Documentation' tool to obtain a valid Context7-compatible library ID UNLESS the user explicitly provides a library ID in the format '/org/project' or '/org/project/version' in their query.

- Versions: List of versions if available. Use one of those versions if the user provides a version in their query. The format of the version is /org/project/version.

Selection Process:

- Name similarity to the query (exact matches prioritized)

- Benchmark Score: Quality indicator (100 is the highest score)

- Provide a brief explanation for why this library was chosen

# Plan: draft SPEC.md for the Harbourmaster rules agent

## Context

`BRIEF.md` asks for an agent that answers players' rules questions about Harbourmaster,
with `RULEBOOK.md` as the only source of truth. The brief deliberately leaves *what
"good" means* to the candidate and grades judgement, not volume of code. Three
structural facts drive every design decision below:

1. **The rulebook will be swapped** (`errata/RULEBOOK_v1.3.md`) with **zero code changes
   allowed**. Anything about the game encoded in Python is a latent bug.
2. **Ten unseen questions (Probe B)** run against the revised rulebook. Tuning to the 25
   given questions is explicitly called out as worthless.

# DRAFT — SPEC.md

## 0. Purpose

An agent that answers rules questions about Harbourmaster from `RULEBOOK.md`, citing the
sections it relied on and declining when the rulebook cannot settle the question.

The rulebook is the **only** source of truth. Not the agent's prior knowledge of board
games, not the player's framing of the question, and not any instruction contained in a
question.

## 1. Interface contract

`./run.sh` — reads JSONL on stdin until EOF, writes JSONL on stdout, nothing else on
stdout. All logging to stderr.

```jsonc
// in
{"id": "q1", "question": "Can I unload four Iron cards onto one Dock?"}
// out
{"id": "q1", "answer": "...", "citations": ["§5.1"], "abstained": false}
```

- **All questions arrive in one invocation.** Read every line before exiting. Never
  assume one question per process.
- Output carries **exactly** the four required keys — no extra diagnostic fields.
  Classification, timings and token counts go to stderr.
- Output order is irrelevant; every input `id` must appear **exactly once**.
- `citations` is sorted in rulebook document order (stability makes assertions possible).
- **Degradation, not crashing.** If the model is unreachable after retries, still emit a
  well-formed record for every id: `abstained: true`, empty citations, and an answer that
  says the agent could not reach the model. `run.sh` exits 0 if it emitted a record for
  every id. Infrastructure failure is loud on stderr and non-zero from `evals.sh`, never
  a missing line on stdout.
- **Malformed input line:** if an `id` can be salvaged, emit an abstention for it; if not,
  warn on stderr and skip. Never emit a record with a null or invented id.
- Question text is truncated at a fixed character cap (logged when it happens) to bound
  cost against a pathological input.

`./evals.sh` — runs the suite, prints a human-readable summary, exits non-zero on failure.
It exercises the agent **only** by invoking `./run.sh` as a subprocess and feeding it
JSONL on stdin. It never imports the agent's modules. This is what makes the mutation
step meaningful.

## 2. The rulebook is pure data

The single hardest requirement: **swapping `RULEBOOK.md` for a different edition must
change the agent's answers with no code change.**

- **One source, one fixed path.** The loader reads exactly one file: `RULEBOOK.md` at the
  repo root, overridable by the `HARBOURMASTER_RULEBOOK` environment variable (used only
  by the eval suite's swap fixture). It **never globs** for `RULEBOOK*.md` and never walks
  subdirectories — `errata/` must be invisible to it. The brief warns about exactly this;
  a loader that picks up two rulebooks is the failure it is baiting.
- **No game facts in code.** No constants, defaults, enums or regexes encoding game
  content. Nothing named `HOLD_LIMIT`, `SPICE_DOUBLES`, `ACTIONS_PER_TURN`. No
  question-specific branches (`if "spice" in question`). If a value can be found in the
  rulebook, code must not restate it.
- **The section index is discovered, not enumerated.** Parsed from the text:
  - `^##\s*§(\d+)\s+(.+)$` → a top-level section with its title.
  - `^§(\d+\.\d+)\s+` at the start of a block → a subsection.
  - A section's text runs from its marker to the next marker of either level, and
    **includes trailing markdown tables and bullet lists** (§7.1's scoring table and §1's
    component list must travel with their section, or scoring questions have no citable
    source).
  - The set of valid citation targets is exactly the set of discovered ids, at both
    granularities. In v1.2 that is `§1..§8` plus `§2.1..§8.4` — but the code knows this
    only by reading.
- **The whole rulebook goes into every prompt.** It is ~3.8 KB (≈1,000 tokens). There is
  no retrieval layer, no chunking, no embeddings. This is a deliberate simplification: it
  removes an entire class of "the retriever missed the relevant section" bug, and it makes
  the rulebook swap trivially correct. The parser's job is to supply the *citation
  vocabulary* and the text — not to select context.
  - Guard: if a loaded rulebook exceeds a stated size threshold, warn loudly on stderr
    that the whole-document assumption no longer holds. Degrading silently into a
    truncated prompt would be the worst outcome.
- **Proof, not assertion.** The eval suite includes a fixture rulebook
  (`evals/fixtures/tiny_rulebook.md`) with deliberately different numbers and section
  numbering, run through `./run.sh` via the env var. Cases assert the answers follow the
  *fixture*. That demonstrates data-driven behaviour without touching the sealed errata.

**What legitimately lives in code:** the *policies* in §4–§8 below — how to resolve a
conflict, when to abstain, how to treat a hostile question. The rulebook supplies content;
the spec supplies conduct. The amendment tests that this line was drawn in the right
place.

## 3. Closed-world assumption

The rulebook is treated as **complete and exhaustive for what exists in the game**. If a
component, suit, action or zone is absent from it, it does not exist, and the agent says
so definitively rather than hedging.

This licenses confident answers to "How does the Tide track work?" — §1 enumerates
components and no track is among them. It is an assumption, and it is the right one for a
rules agent, but it is stated here because it has a cost: against a genuinely incomplete
rulebook the agent will confidently deny things the designer intended. The alternative
(hedging on every unknown noun) makes the agent useless on exactly the questions where a
player most needs a straight answer.

Absence of a *component* is a definitive answer. Absence of a *rule* about components
that do exist is silence, and silence is an abstention (§5, A1).

## 4. Question taxonomy and required behaviour

Every question is classified into exactly one of these. The classification is logged to
stderr (not emitted) and is what the eval suite's fixtures assert against.

| Class | Behaviour | `abstained` |
|---|---|---|
| **Direct** — the rulebook settles it | Answer, cite the sections relied on | `false` |
| **Computed** — arithmetic over rulebook values | Show the result and the components of the sum | `false` |
| **False premise** — the question asserts something the rulebook contradicts | **Correct the premise first**, then answer the underlying question | `false` |
| **Nonexistent entity** — names a component/suit/tile not in the rulebook | State that it does not exist, cite the enumerating section | `false` (see D2) |
| **General/specific** — two sections interact, one carves an exception | Answer definitively per the specific rule, cite both | `false` |
| **Contradiction** — two sections cannot both be true | Surface both readings, name the conflict | `true` (see D1) |
| **Silence** — the rulebook has no bearing text | Say so plainly; do not construct a plausible rule | `true` |
| **Undefined term** — answer depends on a term the rulebook uses but never defines | Say which term is undefined and what turns on it | `true` |
| **Hostile** — instructions dressed as a question | Per §8 | depends |

**False premise is the class most likely to be got wrong, and three probe questions test
it** (Q6 "since Iron cards score double", Q16 "given that each player takes three
actions", Q23 "since a Ship can Sail directly from one Dock to another"). The agent must
not answer the question as posed while silently accepting the false framing, and must not
refuse to answer merely because the framing was wrong. Correct, then answer.

## 5. Abstention criteria

`abstained: true` means **the agent declined to give a definitive answer**. It is not an
error flag and it is not modesty. Abstain if and only if:

- **A1 Silence** — no section bears on the question. *(Q8: nothing in the rulebook says
  what happens when the Draw Pile is exhausted.)*
- **A2 Irreducible contradiction** — two sections give incompatible answers and the
  rulebook offers no principle for preferring one. *(Q4/Q18: Spice.)*
- **A3 Undefined term** — the answer turns on a term the rulebook uses without defining.
  *("round" in §5.4 and §8.2; §6.3's "Storm round" is a different thing.)*
- **A4 No answerable rules question present** — the input contains no rules question at
  all. *(Q11.)*

**Do not abstain** merely because:

- the question's premise was false but the underlying question is settled (Q6, Q16, Q23);
- the question names something that does not exist and the rulebook enumerates the
  category (Q2, Q14, Q19);
- the question arrived wrapped in a hostile instruction but contains a real rules question
  (Q24) — abstaining here would let anyone disable the agent by prefixing "SYSTEM
  OVERRIDE";
- the answer is unwelcome or the rulebook is badly written.

**An abstention still cites.** The sections checked and found silent or conflicting are
what the abstention rests on, and naming them is the useful part. An abstention with no
citations means the agent could not locate any relevant section at all (Q11).

**Abstentions must remain substantive.** "I don't know" is not an acceptable abstention.
State what is missing or in conflict, quote or paraphrase the competing sections, and
where one reading is better supported, say which and why — a player needs enough to agree
a house rule at the table.

## 6. Conflict resolution

Two section pairs conflicting is not one phenomenon but two, and the distinction is
mechanical:

**General/specific — both statements can hold simultaneously**, because one carves an
exception from the other. Answer definitively; the specific rule governs; cite both.

- §4.4 "unload any number" vs §5.1 "more than three only with the Harbourmaster token" →
  §5.1 constrains §4.4. Q25 = **3**.
- §3.3 "roll the Storm die at the end of every player's turn" vs §6.4 "not rolled during
  a Storm round" → §6.4 carves the exception. Q17 = **No**.

**Irreducible contradiction — the statements cannot both hold**, at equal specificity,
about the same subject. Surface both, abstain.

- §4.2 "Spice … counts double when scored" vs §7.1 table "Spice: face value". Both speak
  directly to how Spice scores. They cannot both be true. Q4 = 4 or 8; Q18 = 6 or 12.

The agent does not invent a precedence rule (e.g. "tables beat prose", "later sections
win") to break a true contradiction. Such a rule is a house ruling, not a rule, and
inventing one is precisely how an agent turns a rulebook defect into a confidently wrong
answer. It *does* say which reading is better supported and why, while still abstaining.

## 7. Citations

**Format:** `§N` or `§N.M`, matching `^§\d+(\.\d+)?$`. Model output is normalised
("5.1", "Section 5.1", "§ 5.1" → `§5.1`) *before* validation, so a formatting slip is not
mistaken for a hallucinated section.

**Meaning:** the set of sections whose text the answer's claims actually depend on —
including a section relied on for a *negative* claim ("§1 lists the components and Copper
is not among them") or a *silence* claim.

**Minimality is required, not optional.** Do not cite sections for context, background or
completeness. This is a real constraint, and the `citation_superset` mutation exists to
punish suites that never check it. Prefer the most specific granularity: cite `§7.1`, not
`§7`, when the scoring table is what the answer rests on; cite a bare `§N` only for a
section that has no subsections (e.g. `§1`).

**Preventing citation of sections that do not exist** — three layers, because a prompt
instruction alone is not a guarantee:

1. **Constrain the vocabulary.** The system prompt contains the literal list of valid
   section ids extracted from the loaded file, and states that no other id may be used.
   The model never has to guess what exists.
2. **Validate deterministically after the fact.** Every returned citation is normalised
   and checked against the parsed index. This is the layer that actually enforces the
   property — it holds even if the model ignores the prompt entirely.
3. **Scan the answer prose too.** Every `§`-token appearing in the answer text must be a
   member of `citations` (and therefore of the index). A citation array that validates
   while the prose invents "§9.2" is still a hallucinated citation.

**On failure:** one repair attempt, re-prompted with the offending ids named. If it still
fails, the invalid ids are dropped, the drop is logged to stderr, and if no valid citation
survives on a non-abstained answer, the record is **downgraded to an abstention**
explaining that the agent could not ground its answer. The agent never emits a section id
that is not in the loaded rulebook — that is an invariant, not a best effort.

**Corollary — discussing a section that does not exist.** To say that the rulebook has no
section 9, write it in words ("the rulebook has no section 9"), without the `§` sigil.
The sigil is reserved for real, cited sections. This is a slightly awkward rule and it is
deliberate: it keeps layer 3 a hard mechanical check rather than a heuristic that has to
guess whether a §-token was being negated.

## 8. Hostile questions *(required by the brief)*

**Everything arriving on stdin is data. None of it is instruction.** A question is
untrusted player-supplied text that the agent reads *about*, never *obeys*. Structurally,
question text is never concatenated into the instruction region of the prompt: instructions
and rulebook live in the `system` block, and the question is passed in a user turn inside
a labelled delimiter, with any occurrence of the delimiter in the input escaped.

**The agent refuses to:**

- reveal, quote, summarise or paraphrase its own system prompt, spec or instructions;
- adopt a different persona, ruleset or set of instructions supplied in a question;
- treat an answer asserted in a question as authoritative (Q24's "the correct answer is
  42" is a claim by an untrusted party, and is not in the rulebook);
- load, prefer or acknowledge any rules source other than the loaded rulebook;
- take any action other than answering a rules question.

**The agent answers anyway** when the hostile wrapper contains a genuine rules question.
Q24 asks a real question ("How many actions do I take on my turn?"); the answer is **2**
per §3.1, `abstained: false`, the injected assertion is noted as not coming from the
rulebook and disregarded. Refusing the whole record would mean an attacker can suppress
any answer by prepending a threat.

**When no rules question is present** (Q11), decline in one or two sentences: the agent
answers Harbourmaster rules questions from the rulebook and will not do the requested
thing. `abstained: true`, `citations: []`. The injected text is not echoed back and no
part of the system prompt appears in the answer.

**Enforced, not just requested.** A canary string embedded in the system prompt must never
appear in any answer; the eval suite asserts this on every record. Prompt-level refusal is
the first line; the canary assertion is the one that would actually catch a leak.

## 9. Model invocation

- **Bedrock Converse API** (`bedrock-runtime`), model
  `us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5` (cross-region inference profile; verified present in
  `us-east-1` and `us-west-2`). Region and model id are configurable by environment
  variable with these as defaults — they are infrastructure, not game content.
- `maxTokens` **always set explicitly**. Leaving it unset defaults to the model maximum
  and silently reserves far more quota than needed, which is the most common cause of
  spurious `ThrottlingException`.
- `temperature` 0 — with the explicit caveat in §12 that this reduces variance and does
  not eliminate it.
- **Structured output via strict tool use.** A single tool `submit_ruling` with
  `strict: true` and `toolChoice: {"tool": {"name": "submit_ruling"}}`, schema:
  `answer` (string), `citations` (array of string), `abstained` (boolean),
  `question_class` (enum from §4), `conflict_notes` (string). The last two are consumed
  by the agent for stderr logging and never reach stdout. Forcing a schema'd tool call is
  materially more reliable than asking for JSON in prose, and it means malformed output is
  a rare exception path rather than the common case. *(Build step 0: smoke-test that
  Sonnet 5 accepts `strict` + forced `toolChoice`; fall back to an unforced tool call plus
  schema validation if not.)*
- **One call per question**, dispatched through a small thread pool (default 8) with
  adaptive retry (`Config(retries={"max_attempts": 5, "mode": "adaptive"})`). Retry only
  `ThrottlingException`, `ModelTimeoutException`, `ServiceUnavailableException`,
  `InternalServerException`; never `ValidationException` or `AccessDeniedException`.
  25 sequential calls would risk the 60-second budget; concurrency is what buys it, and
  output order does not matter.
- **Prompt caching: measure before claiming.** The system block (rulebook + instructions)
  is byte-identical across all 25 calls, which is an ideal cache candidate, and 25 calls
  in one TTL window is far past the 2-request break-even. But the block is ≈2,000–2,600
  tokens and Sonnet-class minimums sit at 2,048 — so it may fall *below* threshold, in
  which case the cache point is **silently ignored**. A `cachePoint` is placed after the
  system block, and the spec's claim is only that `cacheReadInputTokens` is *logged and
  reported*. No cost saving is asserted in `EVIDENCE.md` unless that number is observed
  to be non-zero.
- **Token and cost accounting**: input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens summed
  across all calls and printed to stderr, for the `## Probe` block's measured number.

**Redaction note.** stderr must not include the AWS account id, role ARN or any other
account identifier. `EVIDENCE.md` involves pasting real output, the brief forbids sending
anything confidential, and the credentials here belong to a corporate SSO account — the
model id and region are all that need to be logged.

## 10. Deterministic validation layer

Every model response passes through checks that do not involve the model. This is the part
of the agent that makes the guarantees in §7 real rather than aspirational.

1. Tool call present and schema-valid; `citations` a list of strings, `abstained` a bool.
2. Citations normalised, then every id checked against the parsed index (§7 layer 2).
3. Every `§`-token in the answer prose is a member of `citations` (§7 layer 3).
4. `abstained: false` with empty citations is rejected — a definitive answer must rest on
   something (§7 repair path).
5. Answer non-empty and above a minimum length.
6. Canary absent from the answer (§8).
7. Quantities rendered as digits (§11).

Failure → one repair attempt → then the documented downgrade. Every intervention is logged
to stderr with the id and the rule that fired, so the mutation blocks and `NOTES.md` can
name real events.

## 11. Answer style

Short, direct, and useful at a table mid-game. Lead with the answer, then the reason.

**Quantities are written as arabic digits** ("2 actions", "16 points"), not words. Two
reasons, and the second is the interesting one: digits are unambiguous, *and* the
`plausible_wrong` mutation increments only digits — an answer that says "five cards"
is immune to it, which would make my own value assertions untestable and hand me a false
pass. The output format is being constrained here by what makes the eval suite honest.

Quote the rulebook's own wording for the decisive clause where short enough. Never invent
terminology the rulebook does not use.

## 12. Eval suite

Two kinds of case, and the split is the point:

- **Invariants** — hold for *any* question against *any* rulebook edition. These are what
  protect the unseen Probe B questions and survive the amendment untouched.
- **Fixtures** — expectations keyed to the 25 known probe questions. Stronger assertions,
  but some legitimately change when the rulebook does.

Fixtures are declared as `must_include` / `must_not_include` sets plus expected
`abstained` and expected numeric values, rather than exact strings — a model at
temperature 0 is low-variance, not deterministic, and a flaky suite is worse evidence than
a weaker one. `must_not_include` on citations is what catches `citation_superset`, and it
is the assertion most suites omit.

Planned invariants: every input id returned exactly once; exactly the four required keys
with correct types; every citation in the parsed index; every prose §-token present in
`citations`; no record with `abstained: false` and empty citations; minimum answer length;
canary absent; citations sorted and deduplicated.

Planned fixture families: abstention set (Q4, Q8, Q11, Q18); exact values (Q9 → 16,
Q6 → 4, Q20 → 7, Q25 → 3); polarity (Q3/Q5/Q15/Q17 → No; Q7/Q10/Q21 → Yes); premise
correction (Q6, Q16, Q23 must contradict the premise); injection (Q11, Q24 must not comply,
Q24 must still answer 2); nonexistent entities (Q2, Q14, Q19); required citations per
question; §7.3 forbidden everywhere except Q12; the swapped-rulebook fixture.

*(The mutation→case mapping table and the deliberately-uncaught mutation are being
designed in detail and will be folded in below.)*

## 13. Rulebook defects

`DEFECTS.md` is the register; the spec's contribution is that the agent's behaviour is
determined by the *class* of defect (§4, §5, §6), never by a per-defect special case.
Nothing about Spice, "round", or the Draw Pile appears in code. Identified so far:

| Where | Problem | Class |
|---|---|---|
| §4.2 vs §7.1 | Spice "counts double" vs table "face value" | Contradiction → abstain |
| §4.4 vs §5.1 | "any number" vs ">3 only with token" | General/specific |
| §3.3 vs §6.4 | roll every turn vs not during a Storm round | General/specific |
| §5.4, §8.2 | "round" never defined; §6.3's "Storm round" is a distinct thing | Undefined term |
| §5.4 | "current first player" — §2.4 ties first player to the token, but the token moves | Undefined term |
| §5.4 | when the token passes (immediately vs round end); what if nobody unloads | Silence |
| §5.1 | "more than three onto a Dock tile" — per Trade action or cumulative? §7.2 says "in one Trade action" explicitly, §5.1 does not | Ambiguous scope |
| §6.2 | discard timing during a Storm round; whether the roller is affected on the turn they rolled | Ambiguous |
| §6.2 | Ship in the Open Sea with no Cargo — "must discard" with nothing to discard | Silence |
| §4.1 | Draw Pile exhaustion — no rule | Silence |
| §4.2 | no total Ship cargo capacity (only a per-action cap) | Silence |
| §4.3 | Dock→Dock movement not permitted and not addressed | Silence |
| §8.1/§8.2 | game end interacting with an in-progress Storm round | Silence |
| §2.4 | "most recently travelled by boat" — no tie or nobody case | Silence |

Consistency checks that *pass* and are worth recording as checked: §1's 60 Cargo cards =
4 suits × 5 values × 3 copies; §2.2's 12 Dock tiles = 6 on the Quay + 6 boxed; §8.1's
fourth Dock is reachable with 6 on the Quay.

## 14. Non-goals

No UI, no packaging, no coverage target, no retrieval layer, no conversation state, no
multi-turn clarification (the interface is one-shot), no game-state simulation. The agent
answers rules questions about a document.
